heading: Twenty-three documents, read and ranked
lead: David sent twenty-three scans in one go. Every one was put through the same test — the surname in all its spellings, then the fifteen places this archive cares about — and then the ones that scored were read. Three were worth a section of their own, five were worth a line, eleven had the places but not the family, and four could not be read at all. The whole list is here because a negative that is written down does not have to be searched again.

top.t: «LOS FRANCESCHI, la pequeña historia de una familia»
top.w: Napoleón Franceschi González, Caracas 2002, revised 2012, 90 pp.
top.text: **The Corsica question, answered from the inside.** A Venezuelan historian's history of his own family, and it is the Corsican branch entire. They came from **Ersa in Cap Corse** — the long northern finger of the island, with its hamlets Cocinco, Botticella, Granaggiolo, Piazza and Poggio — a place whose name is said to come from *arsia*, burnt, because the land was dry and poor and never held two thousand people; so they lived off the sea or they left. **The first generation is Pietro Franceschi, 29 June 1694 – 12 February 1771**, then Gasparo (1721–1799), Francesco Maria (1750–1828), Pietro (1789–1871), and **Simone, born at Ersa 11 March 1826 and dead there 25 March 1907**, who married Caroline Mattei and whose son François Marie went to Venezuela and died at Miranda in Carabobo in 1918. They married Dominici, Mattei, Pietri, Antoni, Giuli, Bonavita, Morazzani, Casabianca, Bonifacio, Colombani, Potentini and Cervini. The road out ran through the French Caribbean — Puerto Rico, Saint Thomas, Trinidad, Haiti — and then to Venezuela; there is a *Centro de Arte Alejandro Franceschi* at Yauco and a village in Puerto Rico called **Córcega**. **Nothing in ninety pages touches Istria.** This archive's Lines page already says Corsica is not this family; here is the proof, written by a Franceschi.

top.t: «Atti» of the Centro di ricerche storiche di Rovigno, vol. 39
top.text: Every hit is **Camillo De Franceschi cited as the authority on Pula** — Carlo's son, of this archive's own Gologorica family — and it hands over a bibliography this site did not have: «La popolazione di Pola nel secolo XV e nei seguenti» (*Archeografo Triestino*, ser. III vol. III fasc. 2, 1907); «L'antica abbazia di S. Maria del Canneto in Pola» (AMSI XXXIX, 1927); «Dante a Pola» (AMSI XLIV, 1932); «Alcuni cenni sugli antichi monasteri femminili di Pola» (AMSI LV, 1954). **And one that matters more than the others: «Testamenti polesani del secolo XV con alcuni cenni sulle antiche casate patrizie di Pola»** — sixteen fifteenth-century Pula wills, transcribed by Camillo, with an account of the old patrician houses of the city. This archive has just opened a southern-Istrian cluster centred on Pula and cannot say where it came from. Camillo went through Pula's fifteenth-century wills a century ago. **That is the next thing to read, and it was written by a cousin.**

top.t: «Istra iz pera Nobilea» — Pietro Nobile's Istrian drawings
top.text: Not about the family, and full of it. **Camillo De Franceschi bought the Nobile drawings for the Provincial Library in two purchases, 1934 and 1941**, from heirs who were keeping them at **Koper**; he wrote the collection's title on its cover, *Viaggio artistico attraverso l'Istria*; the whole collection has recently been digitised at the **Državni arhiv u Rijeci**. **Giulio De Franceschi** appears throughout as an illustrator and documentarist of monuments, and the author judges his drawings of Pula's Golden Gate and of Poreč more informative than Nobile's own. And one sentence is a find in itself: the author says that reading in that library's holdings he repeatedly came upon **the ex libris «De Franceschi – Seghetto»** — books from the country house at Seget, the Cretan family's own library, sitting on the shelves of a public collection in Istria.

lines.text: A very large collection of essays. The hits are bibliographical — Carlo and Camillo cited among the Istrian historians — with a heavy Omiš presence (158 mentions) that belongs to the Dalmatian family's town rather than to any document about them.
Archaeology of the pre-Roman Histri. The surname occurs only in the apparatus. Useful for the deep background of the peninsula and nothing else.
544 mentions of Umag and nine of the surname — the Seget family's own town, but the hits are references rather than records. Worth reading properly for the Cretan branch, and not yet read.
The standard account of Venetian Istria and the repopulation this family arrived in. Cited already on this site; now held in full.

Eight hundred and twelve mentions of Carnia and only six of the surname — which is itself informative. A surname study of the Carnian valleys that does not make much of this name, in the region this archive's own family is said to come from.

none: Eleven more had the places and not the family, and are recorded so that they need not be opened again for this purpose: «Povijest Istre 1797–1918»; Žerjavić on migration into and out of Istria, Rijeka and Zadar; Žutić, «Srbi svi i svuda»; «Mletačka Istra 1374»; «Imotske modre vode» (a hundred and sixty mentions of Imotski, four of the surname); «Romanska krstilnica» at Koper; «istro»; «pismo 2»; «Život i smrt u Puli»; Marković PP 28; and the «Hrvati i Karolinzi» catalogue.
ocr: And four had **no text layer at all**. **Two of them have since been read.** The **Umag** book was put through optical character recognition and gave the Seget chapel, the library, the vendor of 1720 and a coat of arms dated nineteen years before the family is supposed to have arrived; the **Trieste guide of 1869** gave two men of the name living in the city, a retired controller in via Caserma and a merchant in textiles and pitch in via San Spiridione. Both extractions are filed in the library beside their scans, so neither has to be OCR'd again. The remaining two — the **«Hrvati i Karolinzi» catalogue** and **«Piazza Maggiore era troppo piccola»** — are still unread, and neither looks likely to repay the effort.
source_tri: All twenty-three scans supplied by David Defranceski, September 2026, and now in this project's library. Each was converted to text and tested for the surname in five spellings and for fifteen place-names before being read.
